doc.title: Warren Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 23, 1995

chapter: Sound, electronics and the changing scene
title: Decline of club-date and studio work
summary: Fewer places to earn while learning, work polarized, synthesizers and DJs replacing live bands.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: How has the music scene changed for you or has it, since you started? Is it — for our aspiring jazz musicians — is it getting tougher?
Yeah, I feel very sorry for anybody that really wants to start it now. What’s gone, what’s not necessarily gone, I’m starting to sound like my father for heaven’s sake. What’s not

the same is that there are fewer and fewer places to play and earn while you learn. Those club dates that I did, all the little clubs that I used to go and work on a Saturday night, the places I used to go sit in, they’re gone. I mean it’s not to say they won’t come back at some point, but that whole — there used to be so much to do. I could work three or four times a week in New York doing receptions for companies, and they all had a live band. And now you get one guy with a synthesizer and a singer.

Or a DJ. And that part of it’s gone. There’s a lot of bread and butter work that isn’t there anymore. And that means that all that’s happened is that it’s been polarized. You’re either making a lot of money, or you’ve got a day job and you do it for fun, because economically it’s a struggle to stay just in the middle, to just make a living. Now there’s less studio work because the electronics have taken over. You laughed when I said the synth is cheaper, but it’s a major impact on what we do. Sit down with a pencil sometime when you’re watching television at night, and let those commercials go by. Just make a tick every time you hear electronic background and a tick every time you hear a real live music. You are going to find that electronics is getting a lot of the work.

Oh, yeah, even in the pit bands for the touring Broadway shows I’ve seen, you know, now they’ve got six or seven people in the pit and they’re playing, the string section is now a keyboard man. Things change.

Something, I mean it’s a question of taste too. This is an art, and we sell it to people, and as a result it’s, we’re at the mercy of public taste, whichever way it goes. And you can blame marketers for influencing public taste. And sometimes you’re in the right spot and the right time, and sometimes you’re not, you know? I don’t know quite, if anyone has any control over that.
